Next, I need to characterize the swelling: location (midline vs. lateral), mobility, tenderness, and associated systemic symptoms (e.g., fever, weight loss, dysphagia, hoarseness) — all of which help narrow the differential. Asking about location first is most efficient, as midline vs. lateral strongly differentiates thyroid/ductal vs. nodal/salivary origins.

[QUERY] Is the swelling located in the center of your neck (midline), or more to one side (lateral)?

[REFERENCE] N/A

Since self-assessment may be unreliable, the next most efficient step is to perform a targeted physical examination: inspection and palpation of the neck to determine location, size, consistency, mobility, tenderness, and relationship to swallowing (e.g., thyroid lesions typically move with deglutition). This is rapid, non-invasive, and yields immediate, high-yield information. Palpation will also help assess for associated lymphadenopathy or fixation — critical for distinguishing benign from malignant or inflammatory causes.
